title: How Mindfulness Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain mindfulness, tracing the term from the Pali word sati (translated by a British colonial administrator in Ceylon in the 1880s) through Buddhist teachings on equanimity, non-judgment, and the noble truths and suffering. They cover how lay meditation spread in Burma (Letti Sayadaw, Mingun Sayadaw, the British conquest in 1885), the Japanese Zen modernist D.T. Suzuki bringing Zen to the West, the Insight Meditation Society and figures like Goldstein, Kornfield and Salzberg, and Jon Kabat-Zinn's secular mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. They discuss research on effectiveness for stress, anxiety, depression and pain, a study on mindfulness and helping across racial lines, risks such as unearthed trauma, and criticism of "McMindfulness" in corporate and military settings. The episode ends with a listener mail tribute to Ziggy Bombach.

segments.title: Opening banter and shout-out
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about 'ish' slang and Josh plugs his niece Mila's movie No Exit on Hulu, then introduce the topic of mindfulness.

segments.title: Defining mindfulness and the word sati
segments.summary: The hosts trace mindfulness to the Pali word sati, which a British colonial administrator in Ceylon translated as mindfulness in the 1880s. They describe it as present-moment awareness with equanimity and non-judgment.

segments.title: Suffering, craving and the Noble Truths
segments.summary: The hosts connect mindfulness to the Buddhist view that craving causes suffering, the Four Noble Truths, and dukkha, and discuss Thich Nhat Hanh's teaching that suffering cannot be avoided.

segments.title: Mindfulness as a state and breathing practice
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish mindfulness as a state from meditation as a practice, cite John Kabat-Zinn's purposeful attention, and describe breathing techniques for returning to the present, including Chuck's hug breathing.

segments.title: Lay meditation in Burma and Letti Sayadaw
segments.summary: Meditation was historically limited to monks. After the British conquest of Burma in 1885, lay people organized to practice, and monk Letti Sayadaw taught mindfulness to ordinary people around 1911, followed by Mingun Sayadaw.

segments.title: D.T. Suzuki and Zen's arrival in the West
segments.summary: Japanese Buddhist modernist D.T. Suzuki carried Zen Buddhism to America and Europe, shaped by the Meiji Restoration and by Romantic and Transcendentalist influences. Counterculture Beats and Hippies embraced it.

segments.title: Insight Meditation Society and Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR
segments.summary: Goldstein, Kornfield and Salzberg founded the Insight Meditation Society in Massachusetts. Jon Kabat-Zinn secularized mindfulness, developing mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and, with others, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy.

segments.title: Mindfulness and cognitive behavioral therapy
segments.summary: The hosts explain how mindfulness interrupts automatic thoughts and behaviors in CBT, and how detaching from thoughts and emotions helps evaluate them, with the idea that thoughts are transient.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break in the show with light banter about Rory Cochrane and Slater.

segments.title: Does mindfulness work? Studies and racial helping experiment
segments.summary: Controlled trials of MBSR report reduced self-reported anxiety, depression and stress. A study with sham training found mindfulness-trained white participants were more willing to help Black people, crossing in-group lines.

segments.title: Risks: unearthed trauma and unwanted effects
segments.summary: Some people who meditate uncover buried trauma, experience rage or anxiety, or develop anxiety from not reaching expected bliss. A 2019 study reported unwanted effects in about 20 percent of meditators, and a guide recommends a skilled teacher.

segments.title: Physical pain and the two arrows
segments.summary: Meditation may reduce the subjective unpleasantness of pain. The Buddhist two-arrows teaching separates physical pain from the added suffering of worry, and a 2019 review found MBSR may reduce chronic pain severity.

segments.title: Mindfulness in corporations, military, schools, and McMindfulness
segments.summary: Mindfulness spread to corporations, the military, schools and prisons, with US meditation rates rising from about four percent in 2012. Critics argue it was stripped of ethics and used to offload workplace stress, a critique called McMindfulness, with quotes from Virginia Heffernan and Andrew Olendzki.

segments.title: Listener mail: tribute to Ziggy Bombach
segments.summary: A listener named Michael writes about his father Ziggy Bombach, who came to love the show during the pandemic while they fished and gathered spring water in Stokes Forest. Josh and Chuck pay tribute.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and show credits, with a request for listener mail sent to the show's email address.
